# TREATISE
### ON THE
# APPARITIONS
# OF SPIRITS,
### AND
# ON VAMPIRES,
## OR THE REVENANTS
<note>The term "revenants" refers to those who "come back" from the dead, used here as a synonym for vampires and other restless spirits.</note>
## of Hungary, Moravia, &c.

->*By the Reverend Father Dom* AUGUSTIN CALMET,<-
<note>Dom is a title for certain Benedictine and Carthusian monks.</note>
->*Abbot of Senones.*<-
->New edition revised, corrected & augmented.<-
->VOLUME I.<-

# PREFACE.

**THE** great number of authors who have written on the apparitions of angels, demons, and souls separated from the body <note>This phrase refers to ghosts or the spirits of the deceased existing apart from their physical forms.</note> is not unknown to me; and I do not presume enough of my own capacity to believe that I shall succeed better than they have done, or that I will improve upon their insights and discoveries. I am well aware that I expose myself to criticism, and perhaps to the mockery of many readers who regard this subject as worn out and discredited in the minds of philosophers, scholars, and several theologians. Neither should I count on the approval of the common people, whose lack of discernment prevents them from being competent judges in this matter. My goal is not to foment superstition, nor to nourish the vain curiosity of visionaries <note>The author uses "visionaries" here to describe people prone to hallucinations or those who are overly eager to believe in supernatural sightings.</note> and of those who believe without examination everything told to them, as soon as they find something of the marvelous and the supernatural within it. I write only for

As for the so-called <term>free-thinkers</term> <note>original: "esprits forts." In the 18th century, this term referred to skeptics or libertines who prided themselves on rejecting religious dogma and traditional beliefs to appear intellectually superior.</note>, who reject everything just to distinguish themselves and to place themselves above the common people, I leave them in the sphere of their own elevation: they will think of my work whatever they judge appropriate; and as it is not made for them, they likely will not take the trouble to read it.

I undertook this work for my own instruction, and to form for myself a just idea of everything said about the apparitions of **Angels**, of the **demon**, and of **souls separated from the body** <note>This refers to the spirits of the deceased, or ghosts.</note>. I wanted to see to what extent this matter was certain or uncertain, true or false, known or unknown, clear or obscure.

There will even be some among those I have cited that will not easily find credence among many readers; and I am content for them to treat these as if they had not been recorded.

I ask them, however, to exercise a just discernment between facts and examples, after which they may, alongside me, render their judgment: to affirm, to deny, or to remain in doubt.

It seemed very important to me—given the respect every man owes to the truth, and the veneration that a Christian and a priest <note>The author, Antoine Augustin Calmet, was a Benedictine abbot, which informs his perspective on the intersection of faith and empirical evidence.</note> owes to religion—to disabuse the world of the opinions it holds regarding apparitions, if it believes them all to be true; or to instruct it, and to show the truth and reality of a great number of them, if it believes them all to be false. I never had the thought of treating the matter of apparitions <note>In the 18th century, "apparitions" generally referred to any supernatural appearance, including ghosts, spirits, or divine visions.</note> in depth; I have only treated them, so to speak, by chance and by occasion. My first and principal object was to speak of the *Vampires* of Hungary. In gathering my materials on this subject, many were found which concerned apparitions; their great number caused embarrassment <note>The author uses "embarrassment" (French: *l’embarras*) to mean a cluttering or an overabundance of material that threatened to overwhelm his main topic.</note> to this treatise on vampires. I detached a part of them and composed this dissertation on apparitions; there still remains a good number that I could have detached, and so put more order and sequence into this treatise. Many people have taken the secondary for the primary here, and have paid more attention to the first part than to the second—which was, however, the first and principal in my design.

For I confess that I have always been greatly struck by what is told of the vampires or the revenants <note>A "revenant" (from the French *revenir*, meaning "to come back") is a deceased person who is said to return from the grave to haunt the living.</note> of Hungary, Moravia, and Poland; of the <term>vrykolakas</term> <note>The original text uses "brucolaques," a French transliteration of the Greek *vrykolakas*, referring to a harmful undead creature in Greek folklore similar to a vampire.</note> of Greece; and of the excommunicated, of whom it is said that they do not rot. I believed I ought to give it all the attention of which I am capable, and I judged it appropriate to treat this matter in a specific dissertation. After having studied the matter well, and having informed myself as much as I was able, I found in it little solidity and little certainty; this, joined with the advice of several wise and respectable persons whom I consulted, had caused me to entirely abandon my design, and to give up working on a subject that suffers so many contradictions and contains so much uncertainty.

But viewing the matter from another perspective, I took up the pen again, resolved to disabuse the public if I found that what is said of them were absolutely false, showing that all that is uttered on this subject is uncertain, and that one must be very reserved in pronouncing judgment on these vampires, who

I am therefore going to examine this question as a historian, as a philosopher, and as a theologian. -># P R E F A C E.<-

Complaints have been made that I do not **take a side**, and that I do not reach a decision on several **difficulties** <note>Complex theological or historical problems the author has raised regarding the supernatural.</note> that I propose, and that I often leave my reader in **uncertainty** <note>original: "incertitude".</note>.

I do not offer much defense against this **reproach**; I would have much more reason to justify myself if I had committed to a side without a perfect knowledge of the facts, at the risk of embracing error and falling into a greater inconvenience. It is the mark of **wisdom** to suspend one's judgment until one has arrived at a well-established **truth** <note>original: "vérité".</note>.

I have also been warned that certain people have made **jokes** <note>original: "plaisanteries".</note> about some of the facts I have reported. If I had reported them as certain truths, and they provided just cause for mockery, I would plead guilty; but if I cited them as **fabulous** and false, they are not a subject for humor: ***falsehood is not a source of wit*** <note>original: "falsum non est de ratione faceti"; a Latin maxim suggesting that there is no cleverness or irony in mocking something that is already acknowledged by the author to be a fiction.</note>.

I have been reproached for reporting several **false stories**, several **doubtful facts**, and several **fabulous events** <note>original: "événemens fabuleux"; accounts involving the supernatural or mythological that lack historical or scientific evidence.</note>: it is true; but I only present them for what they are. I have declared several times that I am not their guarantor <note>The author is stating he does not vouch for the truth of these stories.</note>, and that I reported them only to expose their falsehood and ridicule, and to strip them of the credit they might hold in the minds of the common people. If I have not gone into great length to refute them, I believed I should leave that pleasure to my reader, assuming he possesses enough common sense and ability to form his own judgment and to treat them with the same contempt that I do. It would be doing too much honor to certain things to refute them seriously.

I respond that the conclusions drawn from principles are only valid when the circumstances are equal, and the subjects and context are the same; without this, there can be no application of principles. The facts to which my reasoning applies are reported by authors of little authority, by ordinary historians, who possess no character that merits a <term>credibility</term> <note>original: "créance"; the level of trust or belief one places in a witness or text.</note> beyond that of human testimony. I can, without attacking their person or their merit, suggest that they may have been poorly informed, prejudiced, or deceived; that a spirit of deception may have played a part; and that the senses, the imagination, and **superstition** may have caused what was merely apparent to be taken for truth.

# CHAPTER II.

## *Apparitions of good Angels, proven by the Books of the New Testament.*

The books of the New Testament are likewise filled with accounts that prove the apparitions of good Angels. The Angel Gabriel appeared to Zacharias, father of John the Baptist, and predicted to him the future birth of the Precursor (a) <note>Zacharias was a priest; the "Precursor" refers to John the Baptist, who paved the way for Jesus.</note>. The Jews who saw Zacharias come out of the Temple, after he had remained there longer than usual, and having noticed that he had become mute, did not doubt that there had been some apparition of an Angel. The same Gabriel announced to MARY the future birth of the Messiah (b). JESUS having been born in Bethlehem, the Angel of the Lord appeared to the Shepherds during the night (c), and declared to them that the Savior of the world was born in Bethlehem. There is every reason to believe that the star which appeared to the Magi in the east, and which led them straight to Jerusalem, and from there to Bethlehem, was directed by a good Angel (d). Saint Joseph was warned by a celestial Spirit to withdraw to Egypt with the Mother and the Child JESUS, for fear that Jesus might fall <note>The text likely continues to describe the threat from King Herod.</note>

# CHAPTER III.

### *In what form have the good Angels appeared?*

The most common manner in which the good Angels appear in the Old and New Testament is in human form; it is in this form that they showed themselves to Abraham, to Lot, to Jacob, to Moses, to Joshua, to Manoah <note>original: "Manué"</note>, father of Samson, to David, to Tobit <note>original: "Tobie"</note>, and to the Prophets: and in the New Testament they appeared in the same form to the Holy Virgin, to Zechariah, father of Saint John the Baptist, to Jesus Christ after his forty-day fast, and to the same in the Garden of Olives during his agony. They showed themselves in the same way to the holy women after the resurrection of the Savior. The one who appeared to Joshua (a) on the plain of Jericho showed himself apparently in the form of a warrior, since Joshua asked him: *Are you for us, or for our enemies?*

Sometimes they hide themselves under some form that has no relation to the human figure, such as the one who appeared to Moses in the burning bush (b), and who led the Israelites in the desert under the form of a pillar of

## CHAPTER IV.

->Sentiments of the Jews, Christians, 
Muslims, and Eastern peoples concerning 
the appearances of good Angels.<-

After everything we have just related from the books of the Old and New Testament, one cannot deny that the common people among the Jews, the Apostles, the Christians, and their disciples generally believed in the appearances of good Angels. The Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect known for denying the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits or angels</note>, who denied the existence and the appearances of Angels, were considered by the common Jews as heretics, and as upholding an erroneous doctrine. Jesus Christ refuted them in the Gospel.

Modern Jews believe literally what is recounted in the Old Testament regarding the Angels who appeared to Abraham, to Lot, and to the other Patriarchs. This was also the belief of the Pharisees and the Apostles in the time of our Savior, as is seen in the writings of the Apostles and in the Gospel.

The Muslims <note>original: "Mahométans"</note> believe, like the Jews and the Christians, that good Angels sometimes appear to men in human form; that they appeared thus to Abraham and to Lot; that they punished the inhabitants of Sodom; that the Archangel Gabriel appeared to Muhammad (*a*), and revealed to him what he relates in his Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note>; that genies <note>original: "génies," referring to the Jinn of Islamic theology</note> are of an intermediary nature between man and Angel (*b*); that they drink, eat, procreate, die, and foresee future things. As a consequence of this principle, they believe there are male and female genies; that the males, to whom the Persians give the name *Dives* <note>original: "Dives," referring to the Daevas or Divs of Persian mythology—often depicted as monstrous or demonic spirits</note>, are evil, very ugly, and malicious, making war upon the *Peris*, who are the females <note>The author characterizes "Peris" as female genies, though in Persian lore they are more broadly understood as fairylike, benevolent spirits</note>. The Rabbis maintain that these genies were born of Adam alone, without the involvement of his wife Eve, nor of any other woman, and that they are what we call sprites <note>original: "esprits follets," refers to pucks, hobgoblins, or playful, mischievous spirits</note>.

<page-num>19</page-num>
->### ON SPIRITS.<-

The antiquity of these opinions concerning the **corporeality** <term>the state of having a physical, material body</term> of Angels appears in several ancient authors. These writers, deceived by the authority of the apocryphal book <note>religious texts not included in the official biblical canon</note> which circulated under the name of Enoch, applied to Angels what is said in Genesis (a) *that the sons of God, having seen the daughters of men, were enamored by their beauty, married them, and fathered the giants.* Several of the ancient fathers (b) embraced this sentiment, which today is abandoned by everyone, with the exception of a few modern writers who have wished to revive the opinion of the corporeality of Angels, demons, and souls. This sentiment is absolutely incompatible with that of the Catholic Church, which maintains that Angels are of a nature entirely detached from matter.

I acknowledge that in their system, the matter of apparitions would be explained more conveniently: it is easier to conceive of a physical substance appearing and making itself sensible to our eyes than a purely spiritual substance. But it is not appropriate here to reason upon a philosophical question on which one is free to propose different hypotheses, and to choose the one that would most plausibly explain appearances, and which re-

The question is resolved, and the matter decided. The Church and the Catholic schools <note>Referring to the established theological universities and centers of doctrine</note> hold that Angels, demons, and **rational souls** <term>human souls capable of reason, as opposed to animal spirits</term> are free from all matter; the same Church and the same schools hold it as certain that good and bad Angels, and souls separated from the body, sometimes appear by the will or the permission of God. One must hold to this; and as for the manner of explaining these apparitions, one must—without losing sight of the certain principle of the **immateriality** <term>the state of having no physical substance</term> of these substances—explain them according to the analogy of the Christian and Catholic faith. One must acknowledge in good faith that in this matter there are depths that we cannot fathom, and captive our minds and our intellects under the obedience that we owe to the authority of the Church, which can neither err nor deceive us.

The apparitions of good Angels and guardian Angels are frequent in the Old as in the New Testament. When the Apostle Saint Peter had left prison through the ministry of an Angel, and came to knock at the door of the house where his brothers were, they believed that it was his Angel, and not he, who was knocking <note>A reference to the Book of Acts 12:15, where the disciples initially mistook the escaped Peter for his spiritual guardian</note>.

# CHAPTER V.

->*Sentiments of the Greeks & the Romans on the appearances of good Spirits.*<-

Iamblichus, a disciple of Porphyry (*b*), is the author from antiquity who has treated most thoroughly the matter of <term>genii</term> <note>from the Latin 'genius,' referring to a protective spirit or divine nature inherent in each person, place, or thing in classical mythology</note> and their appearances. To hear him discourse, it seems that he knows both the spirits and their qualities, and that he maintains an intimate and continual commerce with them.

He <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD), the Neoplatonist philosopher introduced on the previous page</note> claims that the eyes are gladdened by the appearances of the Gods; that those of the Archangels are terrible; those of the Angels are gentler: but when <term>demons</term> <note>original: "démons"; here referring to "daemons," intermediary spirits in Greek philosophy that could be good or helpful, rather than the purely evil beings of later tradition</note> and <term>heroes</term> <note>in the classical sense, "heroes" were a class of semi-divine spirits, often the souls of the illustrious dead, ranking between humans and daemons</note> appear, they inspire dread. The <term>archons</term> <note>from the Greek for "rulers," these were planetary spirits or cosmic governors believed to oversee the material world</note>, who preside over this world, produce an impression of pain and, at the same time, of terror. The appearance of souls is not quite so disagreeable as that of the heroes. There is order and gentleness in the appearances of the Gods, trouble and disorder in those of the demons, and tumult in those of the archons.

When the Gods show themselves, it seems as if Heaven, the sun, and the moon are about to be annihilated; one would believe that the earth cannot resist their presence. At the appearance of an Archangel, there is a trembling in some part of the world; it is preceded by a light greater than that which accompanies the appearances of Angels, while the light is lesser at the appearance of a demon; it diminishes even further when it is a hero who shows himself.

The appearances of the Gods are very luminous; those of the Angels and Archangels are less so; those of the demons are dark, but less so than those of the heroes. The archons, who preside over the most brilliant things in the world, are luminous; but those who are occupied only with material things are

The Greeks and the Romans recognized, as did the Hebrews and the Christians, two kinds of <term>genii</term> <note>original: "génies"; these are not "genies" in the sense of a lamp-spirit, but "daemons" or guardian spirits believed to guide a person's fate</note>, some good and benevolent, and others evil and inclined toward wickedness. These spirits were considered to be good spirits, benevolent spirits (a), and worthy of the worship of those who invoke them. They were sometimes represented in the form of a serpent, and sometimes in the form of a child or a young man. One offered them flowers, incense, cakes, and wine; *pour pure wine for the genius* (b) <note>original: "funde merum genio"</note>. They swore by the name of these spirits (c), *the steward swears by my genius that he has done all things* <note>original: "villicus jurat per genium meum ſe omnia feciſſe"</note>. It was a great crime to commit perjury after having sworn by the genius of the Emperor, says Tertullian (d), *among you, one more quickly commits perjury by all the Gods than by the single genius of Caesar* <note>original: "citiùs apud vos per omnes Deos, quàm per unicum genium Cæſaris perjuratur"</note>. One sees quite often on medals the inscription, *the genius of the Roman people* <note>original: "genium populi Romani"</note>; and when one arrived in a country, one did not fail to adore its genius and to offer it sacrifices. They did the same when they left a Province; they kissed the earth with respect (e).

The figure of the serpent is almost always seen in the magical figures (d) of *Abraxas* and *Abrachadabra*, which were venerated among the ancient Basilidian heretics <note>Followers of Basilides of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher.</note>, who, just like the Manichaeans, recognized two principles of all things: one good, the other evil. *Abraxa* in Hebrew signifies this evil principle, or the Father of evil; *ab-ra-chad-ab-ra*, the Father of evil, the sole Father of evil, or the sole evil principle <note>The author provides a folk etymology common in the 18th century; the actual origins of "Abracadabra" remain debated by linguists.</note>.

St. Augustine (e) remarks that no animal has been more subject to experiencing the effects of enchantments and magic than the serpent, as if to punish it for having seduced the first woman with its deception.

Michael returned to find his companions who were still playing; he won back all the money he had lost and won all of his companions' money as well. ## CHAPTER VII.

### *On Magic.*

**M**any people view everything said about magic, magicians, spells <term>sortilèges: specifically, magic intended to influence fate or discover secrets</term>, and harmful hexes <term>maléfices: acts of "black magic" intended to cause physical harm or crop failure</term> as fables, illusions, and the effects of the imagination of certain weak minds. These people, foolishly biased by the excessive power of the devil, attribute a thousand things to him which are purely natural, but whose physical causes are unknown to them; or else they are the effects of the cunning of certain charlatans who make a trade of imposing upon the simple-minded. These sentiments are supported by the authority of the principal parliaments <note>In 18th-century France, "parlements" were not legislative bodies like the modern UK Parliament, but rather high courts of justice.</note> of the kingdom of France, which recognize neither magicians nor sorcerers, and who never punish those accused of magic or sorcery unless they are convicted of some other crimes. They argue that, finally, the more magicians and sorcerers are punished and sought after, the more of them are found in a country; and that on the contrary, experience shows that in places where they are not believed—

One imputes to the **demon** <note>the devil or an evil spirit</note> a thousand things in which he has no part; one credits him with **predictions**, revelations of secrets, and discoveries that are in no way the effect of his power, nor of his penetration <note>original: "pénétration" — here meaning his keen intellectual insight or ability to perceive hidden things</note>; just as one accuses him of having caused evils, storms, and diseases, which are the pure effects of natural, but unknown, causes.

Nevertheless, it remains true that there are indeed many people who are convinced of the power of the demon, of his influence over an infinity of things and effects attributed to him; that they have consulted him to know the future, to discover secret things, and that they have turned to him to succeed in their projects, to obtain money or favor, and to enjoy their criminal pleasures. ## *Examination of the Case of Hocque, Magician,*

<margin>(a) Mr. de Saint-André, Letter 6, on the subject of magic, etc.</margin>
Mr. de Saint-André, counselor and physician-in-ordinary to the King <note>a formal title for a physician in the permanent service of the French royal court</note>, in his sixth letter (a) against magic, maintains that in the case of Hocque, of whom we have spoken, there is neither magic, nor sorcery, nor any operation of the demon; that the *gogues* <gloss>poisonous baits or charms</gloss> or venomous drugs that Hocque placed in the stables, and by which means he caused the death of the livestock found there, were nothing other than a poisonous composition, which, through its odor and the discharge of its invisible particles <note>original: "parties insensibles," referring to the contemporary scientific theory that materials emitted microscopic "effluvia" or atoms that could affect the health of those nearby</note> poisoned the animals and caused them to die. One only had to remove these drugs to protect the livestock, or move the livestock away from the stable where the poison was located. The difficulty was in discovering where these *gogues* were hidden; the shepherds, the authors of the mischief, taking all sorts of precautions to hide them, knowing that their lives were at stake if they were discovered.

# OF SPIRITS. #

Everyone knows the stories told of the Marsi <note>An ancient Italic people reputed to have magical powers over snakes and the ability to cure snakebites.</note>, a people of Italy, and of the Psylli <note>A Libyan tribe also famous in the ancient world for being immune to snake venom and for their skills as snake charmers.</note>, who possessed the secret of charming serpents. One would say, says Saint Augustine (a), that these animals understand the language of the Marsi, so obedient are they to their orders; they are seen emerging from their caves as soon as the Marsi has spoken. All this can only be done, says the same Father, through the power of the evil spirit, to whom God allows the exercise of this dominion over venomous beasts, especially over the serpent, as if to punish it for what it did against the first woman <note>A reference to the serpent tempting Eve in the Garden of Eden.</note>. Indeed, it is noted that no animal is more exposed to charms and the effects of the magical art than the serpent.

The laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest foundation of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC.</note> forbid charming the harvests of one's neighbor: *he who had enchanted the crops* <note>original: "qui fruges excantasset"</note>. Verrius Flaccus <note>A Roman grammarian and teacher from the 1st century BC.</note> cites authors who assert that the Romans, when they wished to besiege a city, employed their priests to evoke the divinity who presided over that city, by promising to build it a temple in Rome—either similar to the one it occupied in the besieged city, or a little larger—and that proper worship would be rendered to it <note>This ritual was known as *evocatio deorum*, intended to strip a city of its divine protection before an attack.</note>. Pliny says that the memory of these evocations is preserved among the priests, *this rite endures in the discipline of the Pontiffs* <note>original: "durat in Pontificum disciplina id sacrum"</note> (b).

If everything that has just been told, and what one reads about it in both ancient and modern authors, has some reality, and produces the effects attributed to them, one cannot doubt that there is something supernatural involved, and that the demon has a large part in it.

Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German Benedictine abbot, a polymath, and a writer on the occult who was often accused of practicing magic himself.</note> speaks of a witch who, by means of certain potions, changed a young Burgundian <note>A person from the region of Burgundy, France.</note> into a beast.

Everyone knows the fable of Circe <note>The enchantress from Homer’s Odyssey.</note>, who changed the soldiers, or companions of Ulysses, into swine. We also know the fable of the *Golden Ass* by Apuleius <note>A 2nd-century AD Roman novel, also called the "Metamorphoses," about a man who is accidentally turned into a donkey while trying to perform magic.</note>, which contains the account of a man metamorphosed into a donkey. I only present all this for what it is—that is to say, as poetic fictions.

But it is very believable that these fictions are not without some foundation, like so many other fables which contain not only a hidden and moral meaning but also relate to some real, historical event; for example, what is said of the Golden Fleece, captured by Jason; of the wooden horse, which served to surprise the city of Troy; of the twelve labors of Hercules; of the metamorphoses reported in Ovid. All of this, as fabulous as it may appear in the poets, nevertheless has its truth in history. Thus, pagan historians and poets have travestied and disfigured the stories of the Old Testament, and have attributed to Bacchus, to Jupiter,

He strikes the drum with a forked hammer made of bone, in such a way that these rings move; at the same time, he sings a song in a distinct voice, which the Laplanders <note>Historically called "Lapps" in this era, these are the Sami people of Northern Scandinavia.</note> call a *Jouk* <note>original: "Jouk"; this refers to the *joik*, a traditional form of Sami vocal music used in spiritual and social contexts.</note>; and all those of their nation who are present, both men and women, each add their own song, expressing from time to time the name of the place from which they desire to learn some news.

The Laplander, having struck the drum for some time, places it on his head in a certain fashion and immediately falls to the ground motionless, giving no sign of life. All the men and women continue singing without pause until he has come back to himself; if they stop singing, the man dies. This also happens to him if anyone tries to wake him by touching him with their hand or foot. They even keep flies away from him, as their buzzing might wake him and cause him to return <note>The belief was that the shaman's soul had left the body to travel; an abrupt return or a failure to sustain the ritual atmosphere could prove fatal.</note>.

When he has returned to himself, he answers the questions put to him concerning the place where he was sent. Sometimes he does not wake until the end of—

It is not that they were convinced of the truth of what they were saying; they were the first to mock these ideas when the occasion arose, as did the most sensible and wise men of pagan antiquity. But neither the Princes nor the priests took much trouble to disabuse the common people, nor to destroy their prejudices <note>The author uses "prejudices" to describe the irrational beliefs or superstitions held by the masses.</note> regarding all of this. The pagan religion tolerated and authorized these beliefs; many of its practices were founded upon such superstitions.

## CHAPTER XIV.

->*On the Oracles of the Pagans.*<-

If it were well-proven that the oracles of pagan antiquity were the work of the evil spirit <note>The author refers here to the "mauvais esprit" or demon, reflecting the common early modern belief that ancient pagan gods were actually fallen angels or demons deceiving humanity.</note>, one could not provide more tangible and striking evidence of the demon's appearance among men than these much-celebrated oracles. They were delivered in almost every country of the world, among those nations regarded as the wisest and most enlightened—such as the Egyptians, Chaldeans, Persians, Syrians, even the Hebrews themselves <note>This likely refers to periods of idolatry mentioned in the Old Testament, where Hebrews turned to foreign oracles.</note>, the Greeks, and the Romans. There was no people, even among those deemed barbarian, who did not have their oracles.

<margin>(a) Pliny, *Natural History*, Book 8, Chapter 48.</margin>
Pagan religion possessed nothing in which it took greater pride, or of which it boasted with more satisfaction. In all great undertakings, people had recourse to the oracle; by this means, the most important affairs were decided between city and city, and province and province. The manner of delivering these oracles was not the same everywhere. It is said (a) that the bull Apis <note>A sacred bull worshipped in ancient Egypt, specifically in Memphis, as an intermediary between humans and the creator god Ptah.</note>, whose cult is so ancient in Egypt, delivered his oracles by receiving food from the hand of the person who consulted him. If he accepts it, it is said, they draw from this <note>The text cuts off here, but the tradition states that if Apis accepted the food, it was a good omen; if he refused, it was a bad one.</note>

# CHAPTER XVI.

*Reasons that can persuade us that most ancient Oracles were nothing but the trickery of Priests and Priestesses, who feigned being inspired.*

If it is true, as many ancient and modern authors have believed, that the oracles of pagan antiquity were only illusions and deceits on the part of the priests and priestesses, who claimed to be possessed by the spirit of <term>Python</term> <note>original: "esprit de Python"; a reference to the Pythian spirit of the Oracle of Delphi, named after the serpent-dragon Python slain by Apollo</note>, and filled with the inspiration of <term>Apollo</term> <note>The Greek and Roman god of prophecy, music, and light</note>, who internally revealed to them hidden things—past, present, and future—I should not place them here in the rank of apparitions of evil spirits. The <term>demon</term> <note>In this context, the Devil or a malevolent spirit</note> would have no other part in them than that which he has in the crimes of men, and in that multitude of sins that greed, ambition, self-interest, and self-love produce in the world; the demon is always attentive to seducing us and casting us into disorder and error, employing all our passions to draw us into his snares.

If what he has predicted is followed by its fulfillment, whether by chance, or because he foresaw certain circumstances unknown to men, he attributes the glory of it to himself, and uses it to attract ou- <note>The text ends mid-word on the catchword "no-," likely for "notre" (our).</note>

The ancient legislators of Greece, the most skillful politicians, and army generals made clever use of the people’s prejudice in favor of oracles, to persuade them that what they had planned was approved by the Gods and announced by the oracle. These things and these enterprises were often followed by happy success—not because the oracle had predicted or ordered it, but because the enterprise was well planned and well conducted, and because the soldiers, for example, persuaded that God was on their side, fought with a more extraordinary valor.

Arnobius <note>Arnobius of Sicca (d. c. 330 AD), an early Christian apologist who wrote against pagan practices.</note> and Julius Firmicus Maternus <note>A 4th-century Roman senator and Christian convert who wrote "On the Error of Profane Religions."</note> teach that in these festivals a golden serpent was slipped into the breast of those being initiated, and then withdrawn from below; but this etymology is far-fetched. # CHAPTER XVIII.

## Examples of Sorcerers and Witches Supposedly Transported to the Sabbath.

Everything said about witches going to the Sabbath <note>A "Sabbath" in this context refers to a secret nocturnal gathering of witches, believed in folklore to involve dancing, feasting, and worship of the Devil</note> is treated as mere fables, and we have several examples which prove that they do not stir from their beds nor their rooms. It is true that some rub themselves with a certain grease or ointment <term>onguent: a medicinal or magical salve; historical "flying ointments" often contained hallucinogenic plants like belladonna or henbane</term> which makes them drowsy and renders them insensible; and during this fainting fit, they imagine they go to the Sabbath, and there see and hear what everyone says is seen and heard there.

One reads in the book titled *Malleus maleficarum* <note>original Latin: "Malleus maleficarum", translated as the *Hammer of Witches*, a famous and influential treatise on the prosecution of witches written in 1486</note>, or *Hammer of Witches*, that a woman assured the inquisitors <note>Officials of the Inquisition, a judicial institution of the Catholic Church tasked with suppressed heresy</note> into whose hands she had fallen, that she truly and bodily transported herself wherever she wished, even though she was locked up and closely guarded, and even if the place where she went was very far away.

The inquisitors ordered her to go to a certain place, to speak to certain people, and to bring back news of them; she promised to obey. They locked her in a room under key; immediately she lay down

# ON SPIRITS.

If one could rely on all these stories, and on an infinity of other similar ones that are told, and of which books are full, one might believe that sometimes sorcerers are carried bodily to the Sabbat <note>A legendary midnight assembly of witches and sorcerers</note>; but in comparing these stories with others which prove that they only go there in spirit and in imagination, one can assert that everything told of sorcerers and witches, who go or believe they go to the Sabbat, is usually nothing but illusion on the part of the devil, and seduction <note>In this context, "seduction" refers to being led astray or deceived by false appearances.</note> on the part of those men and women who imagine themselves flying and traveling, although they do not stir from their places. The spirit of malice and lies mingling with this foolish prejudice, they confirm themselves in their wanderings, and they involve others in their impiety; for Satan has a thousand ways to deceive men and keep them in their errors. Magic, impieties, and <term>maléfices</term> <note>harmful magic or spells intended to cause misfortune, illness, or death</note> are often the effect of disorders of the imagination. It is rare that these sorts of people do not fall into all the excesses of unchastity, irreligion, theft, and all the most extreme consequences of hatred for one's neighbor.

Some have believed that demons took the form of the sorcerers and witches who were thought to attend the Sabbat <note>A legendary midnight assembly where witches were said to worship the devil</note>, and that they kept simple-minded people in this foolish persuasion by appearing to them at times in the likeness of those persons reputed to be witches, while the people themselves rested peacefully in their beds. But this belief holds difficulties as great as, or perhaps greater than, the opinion one intends to challenge. It is very difficult to understand why the demon would take the form of these alleged sorcerers or witches—why he would appear in this form, why he would drink, eat, and travel—all for the sake of making simple people believe that sorcerers go to the Sabbat. What advantage does the demon gain by persuading idiots of this, or by keeping them in such an error?

After this dialogue, the father asked her how she would go about making it rain only upon his field; she asked only for a little water. He led her to a nearby stream, and the girl, having called upon the water in the name of the one to whom her mother had dedicated her, an abundant rain was immediately seen falling upon the peasant's field.

The father, convinced that his wife was a witch, accused her before the judges, who condemned her to the fire <note>Being "condemned to the fire" refers to execution by burning at the stake, the standard punishment for heresy and witchcraft in many jurisdictions.</note>. The little girl was baptized and dedicated to God; but she then lost the power to make it rain at her will.

## CHAPTER XIX.

### *The History of Louis Gaufredi and Magdeleine de la Palud, Self-Confessed Sorcerer and Sorceress.*

<margin>(a) *Famous Cases*, Vol. 6, p. 192. <note>original title: "Causes célèbres." This refers to the collection of famous legal trials compiled by François Gayot de Pitaval in the 18th century.</note></margin>

Here is a notable example of a man and a woman who declared themselves to be a sorcerer and a sorceress. Louis Gaufredi, the parish priest of the Accoules <note>The Church of Notre-Dame-des-Accoules is one of the oldest churches in Marseille.</note> in Marseille, was accused of magic and arrested at the beginning of 1611 (*a*). Christophe Gaufredi, his uncle and the priest of Pourrières <note>A village in the Provence region of France.</note>, a neighbor of Beauversas, sent him a small sixteen-mo <term>sixteen-mo</term> <note>A book size where each sheet is folded to create sixteen leaves, making for a very small, portable volume.</note> booklet of six written leaves six months before his death. At the bottom of each leaf there were two French verses; the work contained many characters or ciphers that held the mysteries of magic. Louis Gaufredi initially paid little attention to this book and kept it for five years without reading it.

At the end of this time, having read the French verses, the devil presented himself to him in a human form, not at all deformed, and told him that he had come to fulfill all his desires if he would hand over all his good works to him. Gaufredi gave him his written pledge <note>In historical accounts of witchcraft, the "billet" or "pact" was a signed contract promising the soul to the devil in exchange for power.</note>; he asked the demon that he might enjoy a great reputation for...

This girl was only nine years old, and Gaufredi—under the pretext of devotion and spirituality, having made her understand that as her spiritual father he had the right to dispose of her—engaged her also to give herself to the demon; and a few years later, he forced her to give a bond <term>cedule</term> <note>From the French 'cédule', a formal written document or contract; in occult accounts, this refers to a signed diabolical pact.</note> signed with her own blood to the devil, to surrender herself more and more to him. It is even said that he later made her create seven or eight other bonds.

After this, he breathed upon her, inspired a violent love for himself in her, and abused her; he gave her a familiar demon <note>A 'familiar' was believed to be a lower-level spirit or entity that served and accompanied a witch or sorcerer.</note> who served her and followed her everywhere. One day, he transported her to the Sabbat <note>A secret midnight assembly of witches and sorcerers.</note> on a high mountain near Marseille. There she saw people of all nations, and particularly Gaufredi, who held a very distinguished rank there. He had magical characters <note>Magical symbols or sigils, often called 'the devil's mark' in witchcraft trials.</note> imprinted upon her head, her face, and on several other parts of her body. This girl later became a nun of the Order of Saint Ursula and was regarded as being possessed by the demon.

Opinions are very much divided on the matter of demonic obsessions and possessions. The hardened Jews and the ancient enemies of the Christian religion, convinced by the evidence of the miracles they saw performed by Jesus Christ, his Apostles, and the Christians, dared not contest either their truth or their reality: they attributed them to magic, to the prince of demons, or to the power <note>original: "vertu" — here meaning the inherent medicinal or magical property</note> of certain herbs or certain natural secrets.

Saint Justin, Tertullian, Lactantius, St. Cyprian, Minucius, and the other Fathers of the first centuries of the Church speak of the dominion that Christian exorcists exercised over the possessed in a manner so full of confidence and freedom that one cannot doubt either the certainty or the evidence of the matter. They call their adversaries as witnesses and make it a point to perform the experiment in their presence, forcing the demons to leave the bodies of the possessed, to declare their names, and to acknowledge that what is worshiped in the temples of the pagans are nothing but demons.

Some opposed the true miracles of the Savior with those of their false gods, their magicians, and the heroes of paganism, such as those of Aesculapius <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine and healing.</note> and the famous Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher often compared to Jesus by pagan authors due to his reported miracles and wandering lifestyle.</note>.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### *The truth and reality of demonic Possessions and Obsessions,*
### *proven by Scripture.*

But the possibility, truth, and reality of demonic obsessions and possessions are beyond doubt, being proven by Scripture and by the authority of the Church, the Church Fathers, the Jews, and the pagans. Jesus Christ and the Apostles believed this truth, and they taught it publicly. The Savior offers as proof of his mission that he heals the possessed; he refutes the Pharisees, who claimed that he only drove out demons in the name of Beelzebub <note>Beelzebub is a name derived from a Philistine god, used in the New Testament as another title for Satan or the prince of demons</note>, and he maintains that he casts them out by the power of God, *by the finger of God* <note>original Latin: "in digito Dei"</note> *(a)*. He speaks to the demons who possessed the energumens <term>energumen: a historical term for someone believed to be possessed by a demon or "worked upon" by an external spirit</term>, he threatens them, and he commands them to be silent. # CHAPTER XXIV.

## *Remarkable Examples of Possessions & Obsessions.*

It is now necessary to recount some famous examples of demonic possessions and obsessions. Today, everyone speaks of the possession of the nuns of Loudun <note>The Loudun possessions of 1634 involved a convent of Ursuline nuns who accused a local priest, Urbain Grandier, of witchcraft; it remains one of the most famous cases of mass hysteria and political intrigue in French history.</note>, regarding which so many diverse judgments were made, both at the time and since then. Marthe Brossier <note>The original text spells her name "Broffier," likely due to the historical use of the "long s" (ſ), which resembles an "f." Brossier was a famous late 16th-century claimant of possession.</note>, the daughter of a weaver from Romorantin (a), also caused a great sensation in her time. During the reign of Charles IX <note>King of France from 1560 to 1574; his reign was defined by the brutal religious conflicts between Catholics and Huguenots.</note>, who died in 1574, or shortly before, a young woman from the town of Vervins, aged fifteen or sixteen years and named Nicole Aubry, had several appearances of a specter. This spirit claimed to be her grandfather and asked her for masses and prayers for the repose of his soul (a). Soon after, it happened that she was transported to various places by this specter, and sometimes even carried away in the sight and from the midst of those who were guarding her.

At that point, there was no longer any doubt that it was the devil, although it took a great deal of effort to persuade her of this. The Lord Bishop of Laon <note>Jean de Bours, the Bishop of Laon, who conducted public exorcisms of Nicole Aubry in 1566 in what became known as the "Miracle of Laon."</note> gave his authority to conjure this spirit, and commanded that care be taken to ensure that the official reports were exactly drawn up by the notaries appointed for this purpose. The exorcisms lasted more than three months and served only to confirm the possession more and more. The poor sufferer was snatched from the hands of nine or ten men who had great difficulty in restraining her; and on the last day of the exorcisms, sixteen could hardly manage her; lying

# APPARITIONS

An event so important and so carefully documented—whether by the Bishop and the Cathedral Chapter, or by the city Magistrates, and even through the public outcries of the Calvinist party <note>Calvinists were French Protestants (Huguenots) who followed the teachings of John Calvin; they were often the primary skeptics of Catholic miracles during this period.</note>—ought not to be buried in silence. When King Charles IX <note>Charles IX: King of France (reigned 1560–1574) during the height of the French Wars of Religion.</note>, making his official entry into Laon some time later, wished to be informed about it by the Dean of the Cathedral, who had been an eyewitness to the events. His Majesty ordered him to publish the history of the matter; it was thus printed first in French, and later in Latin, Spanish, Italian, and German, with the approval of the Sorbonne <term>Sorbonne: the prestigious theological faculty of the University of Paris, serving as the highest authority on Catholic doctrine in France</term>, and supported by the rescripts <term>rescripts: official written responses from a Pope regarding matters of law or doctrine</term> of Popes Pius V and Gregory XIII, his successor. Since then, a fairly accurate summary has been produced by order of the Bishop of Laon, printed under the title: *The Triumph of the Holy Sacrament over the Demon.*

Here, then, is a fact that possesses all the authenticity one could desire—so much so that a man of honor cannot decently cast it into doubt, for after doing so, he could no longer hold any historical facts as certain without shamefully contradicting himself.

In Lorraine, around the year 1620, there was a possessed woman who caused a great stir in the country, but who is much less known among foreigners. # CHAPTER XXVI.

## *Objections against Demonic Obsessions and Possessions. Responses to these Objections.*

Many objections can be raised against the <term>obsessions</term> <note>In the theology of the time, "obsession" referred to external harassment by a demon (such as terrifying sounds or physical blows), as opposed to "possession," where the demon was thought to reside inside the body.</note> and the possessions of demons; no subject is more prone to great difficulties than this matter. However, it is a constant and uniform conduct of <term>providence</term> <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power.</note> to allow the clearest and most certain truths of religion to remain shrouded in some obscurities; to allow the most constant and indubitable facts to be subject to doubts and contradictions; and to allow the most evident miracles to be contested by certain <term>unbelievers</term> <note>The original French "incrédules" refers to skeptics or those who doubt religious dogma.</note> based on circumstances that appear to them doubtful and debatable.

Jesus Christ in the Gospel refutes those who said that he cast out demons in the name of Beelzebub (a) <note>Beelzebub, originally a Philistine deity ("Lord of the Flies"), is used in the New Testament as a name for the prince of demons or Satan.</note>; he maintains that the accusation is ill-founded, because it was not believable that Satan would destroy his own work and his empire. One might object against this reasoning that Jesus Christ assumed, like the Jews, that the demons he cast out really possessed those he cured, in whatever manner he cured them, and consequently that the empire of demons subsisted, both in Beelzebub, prince of demons, and in the other demons who were subordinate to him and obeyed his orders: thus his empire was not entirely destroyed, in supposing that Jesus Christ cast them out in the name of Beelzebub; on the contrary, this subordination presupposed this empire of the prince of demons, and strengthened it.

It recognized this in its decisions in the year 1518, and even more positively on January 23, 1724: *“We respond to your petition that it is well-established that the souls of the deceased return at times to the living through divine power, or by divine strength, ordination, or permission.”* <note>original Latin: "Nos respondemus vestræ petitioni animas defunctorum divinitùs, seu divinâ virtute, ordinatione aut permissione, interdum ad vivos redire exploratum esse."</note> Several legal experts and several sovereign companies <note>In this context, "sovereign companies" refers to the high courts of justice in France, such as the Parlements, which had the authority to issue definitive rulings.</note> have judged that the appearance of a dead person in a house could justify the termination of lease agreements <term>baux à loyer: rental contracts or leases</term>. It should be considered a great achievement to have proven to certain people that there is a God whose providence extends over all things past, present, and future; that there is another life, with good and evil spirits, rewards for good works, and punishments after this life for sins; and that Jesus Christ has ruined the reign of Satan—an authority He exercised Himself, through His Apostles, and which He continues to exercise through the ministers of His Church.

We have seen a deaf person who understood what one wanted to say to him, by seeing only the movement of the lips of the person speaking to him. There is no more miracle in that than in those who speak to each other by signs upon which they have agreed.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

### *Hobgoblins, or Familiar Spirits.*

**I**f everything recounted about hobgoblins <note>original: *esprits folets*. These refer to "frolicsome spirits" or mischievous entities like pucks, brownies, or poltergeists traditionally thought to inhabit domestic spaces.</note>, who make themselves felt in houses, in the hollows of mountains, and in mines, is well-attested, one cannot deny that they must also be ranked among the apparitions of the evil spirit. For although they usually do no harm or violence to anyone, unless they are provoked or insulted with words, we nevertheless do not read that they lead one to fear or love God, nor to prayer, piety, or acts of religion. On the contrary, it is known that they demonstrate an aversion to these things; thus, we shall not hesitate to place them among the spirits of darkness.

I do not observe that the ancient Hebrews knew of what we call hobgoblins, or familiar spirits <note>original: *esprits familiers*. In early modern belief, these were supernatural entities believed to attend to or protect a specific person, often appearing in animal form or as invisible voices.</note>, who infect houses or attach themselves to certain people to serve them, warn them, and protect them from dangers—such as the spirit of Socrates <note>Known as the *daimonion* of Socrates, a divine inner voice that warned him against making mistakes.</note>, which warned him to avoid certain misfortunes. A few other examples are also recounted of people who claimed to have similar geniuses <note>original: *génies*. From the Latin *genius*, a guardian spirit assigned to a person at birth.</note> attached to their persons.

Cassian (*a*), who had extensively studied the lives of the Desert Fathers and who had frequently visited the hermits of Egypt, recognizes—while speaking of various kinds of demons—that there are some commonly named *Fauns* or *Satyrs*. Everyone acknowledges that there is an infinite amount of wealth buried under the earth, or lost under the waters through shipwrecks; it is imagined that the demon—whom people regard as the God of wealth, the God *Mammon*, the Pluto of the pagans—is the custodian, or at least the guardian, of these treasures. Job seems to allude to this ancient custom when he says (*a*): *Would to God that I had never been born; I would now be sleeping with the Kings and the Great Men of the earth who have built solitudes <note>In this context, "solitudes" refers to isolated, magnificent tombs or monuments built in desolate places.</note> for themselves, like those who seek a treasure, and who are delighted when they have found a tomb;* undoubtedly because they hope to find great riches there.

There were very precious things in the tomb of Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great (c. 600–530 BC), the founder of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.</note>. If treasures have been placed in the mausoleums of good and holy people, and if they have been found upon the indication of good spirits—of people who died in the faith and in the grace of God—one cannot conclude that all hidden treasures are in the power of the demon, or that he alone has knowledge of them. The Prelate offered the Holy Sacrifice <note>The celebration of the Mass or Eucharist.</note>, participated in it, and having gone to the site, scattered the demons, guardians of these riches, and put the King in peaceful possession of the castle.

# CHAPTER XXXII.

## *Specters who appear, and who predict future and hidden things.*

**WE** find in the works of the ancients and the moderns an infinite number of stories regarding specters. We do not doubt that their appearances are the work of the demon <note>original: "démon"; in this 18th-century context, the author refers to malevolent supernatural entities or the Devil, as was standard in theological treatises on the paranormal.</note>, if they are indeed real. However, one cannot deny that there are many illusions and falsehoods in all that is told to us. We shall distinguish here between two sorts of specters: some who appear to men to harm them, or to deceive them, or to announce future things to them, whether fortunate or troublesome, depending on the circumstances; other specters infest certain houses, of which they have made themselves masters, and where they make themselves seen and heard. We shall treat these latter ones in a separate chapter, and we shall show that the majority of these specters and these apparitions are highly suspected of being false.

Quintus Curtius Rufus <note>A Roman politician and historian of the 1st century AD. This specific story is recorded by both Tacitus (Annals 11.21) and Pliny the Younger.</note>, who, having traveled to Africa in the suite of the quaestor <note>A Roman official responsible for financial administration.</note> or treasurer on behalf of the Romans, was walking one evening under a portico when he saw a woman of extraordinary height and beauty. She told him that she was "Africa" and assured him that he would one day return to this same country in the capacity of proconsul <note>A governor of a Roman province.</note>. This promise inspired great hopes in him; and upon his return to Rome, he exerted such effort through his intrigues and the help of friends he had won over with money, that he obtained the quaestorship, and subsequently the praetorship <note>An elective judicial office in ancient Rome, second only to the consulship.</note> through the favor of the Emperor Tiberius.

Since this dignity covered the obscurity and lowliness of his birth, he was later sent as proconsul to Africa, where he died after receiving the marks of honor of a triumph <note>A "triumph" was the highest honor for a Roman general, a spectacular public parade through Rome to celebrate military victory.</note>. It is said that upon his return to Africa, the same figure who had predicted his future greatness appeared to him again at the moment of his landing at Carthage.

These predictions, so precise and so exactly followed by the event, led the young Pliny to believe that these sorts of prognostications are not always in vain. This story of Curtius Rufus had been written by Tacitus quite a long time before Pliny, who might well have taken it from Tacitus.

Julius Caesar *(a)*, being ready to enter Italy and cross the Rubicon, perceived a man of an extraordinary height, who began to whistle. Several soldiers having run forward to hear him, this specter seized the trumpet from one of them, and began to sound the alarm and cross the river. At this moment Caesar, without further deliberation, said: Let us go where the omens of the Gods and the injustice of our enemies call us. <note>original: *Allons où les présages des Dieux & l’injustice de nos ennemis nous appellent.* This translates the Latin phrase "Eatur quo deorum ostenta et inimicorum iniquitas vocat," famously attributed to Caesar by Suetonius.</note>

The Emperor Trajan *(b)* was drawn out of the city of Antioch by a phantom, who made him exit through a window in the midst of that terrible earthquake which overturned almost the entire city. <note>This earthquake occurred in 115 AD; the historian Cassius Dio records that a figure of superhuman size led Trajan to safety.</note> The philosopher Simonides *(c)* was warned by a specter that his house was about to fall; he left it immediately, and soon afterward it collapsed.

The Emperor Julian the Apostate <note>Julian (reigned 361–363 AD) was the last non-Christian emperor of Rome; he attempted to revive traditional Roman polytheism.</note> told his friends that while his troops were pressing him to accept the Empire while he was in Paris, he saw a specter during the night in the form of a woman, as the <term>Genius<gloss>In Roman belief, a *Genius* was a guardian spirit or divine nature that accompanied a person or an institution throughout its existence.</gloss></term> of the Empire is depicted. Dion the philosopher, a disciple of Plato and General of the Syracusans, was sitting one evening, deep in thought, in the portico of his house, when he heard a loud noise; he then perceived a terrible specter of a woman of monstrous size, who resembled a Fury <note>In Greek mythology, the Furies (or Erinyes) were deities of vengeance often depicted in tragedies as terrifying women with snakes for hair.</note>, such as they are depicted in tragedies. Marcus Brutus, one of the murderers of Julius Caesar, was in his tent during a night that was not very dark; toward the third hour of the night <note>Approximately midnight, according to the Roman system of dividing the night into four watches.</note>, he saw a monstrous and terrible figure enter. # CHAPTER XXXIV.

## *Examination of the Apparition of a Purported Specter.*

<margin>
(a) Life of Gassendi, vol. 1. page 258.

**Business** (a) having led the Count of Alais (b) to Marseille, a most extraordinary adventure befell him. He immediately instructed Neuré <note>Jean Neuré was a close friend and biographer of the philosopher Gassendi.</note> to write of it to Mr. Gassendi <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher, priest, and astronomer who sought to reconcile atomism with Christian doctrine and was known for his skeptical empirical approach.</note>, to know what he thought of it; which he did in these terms: The Count and the Countess, having come to Marseille, saw while lying in their bed a luminous specter; they were both very much awake. To better ensure it was not some illusion, they called their valets; but these had no sooner appeared with their torches than the specter vanished. They had all the openings and cracks they could find in the room blocked up, and returned to bed: hardly had the valets withdrawn when the specter reappeared.

Gassendi, consulted on this matter, replied on the 13th of the same month. He began by stating that he did not know what to think <note>The OCR reads "ne fait que croire," but in this period’s idiom, it likely intended "ne sait que croire"—meaning he was at a loss for an explanation.</note> of this vision. He did not deny that this specter might have been sent by God to teach the Count of Alais <note>Louis de Valois, Count of Alais (1596–1653), was a high-ranking French nobleman and the Governor of Provence.</note> something. What made this view probable was the great piety of the Prince and the Princess, and the fact that this specter was not frightening, but rather the opposite. However, what deserves even more of our attention is that if God had sent it, He would have made known the reason for sending it. God does not toy with us; and since one cannot understand what one is meant to hope for or fear, to follow or to avoid, it follows that this specter could not have come from Him. Otherwise, His conduct would be less praiseworthy than that of a father, a Prince, a man of virtue, or even a prudent man...

[...proceed from God or good spirits]; who, being informed of something that might greatly interest those subject to them, would not be content to warn them enigmatically.

If this specter is something natural, nothing is more difficult than discovering its cause, or even finding a conjecture to attempt to explain it. Although I am well-convinced of my own ignorance, I will venture my opinion. Could we not suggest that this light appeared because the Count's eye was affected internally, or because it was affected externally? The eye can be affected internally in two ways: first, if his eye were in the same state as that of the Emperor Tiberius <note>The Roman Emperor Tiberius (42 BCE – 37 CE) was described by the historian Suetonius as having eyes so large that they could see in the dark upon first waking, though the effect soon faded.</note>; when this Emperor woke at night and opened his eyes, a brightness would emanate from them, allowing him to discern things in the darkness when he fixed his gaze upon them. I have learned that the same thing happened to a lady of high rank. Secondly, if his eyes were arranged in a certain way, as happens to me myself when I wake: if I open my eyes, they are all radiant with light, even though there was nothing there. No one could deny that some flash might emerge from our eyes which represents objects to us, which objects reflect back into our eyes and leave their traces there <note>This refers to the ancient "extramission theory" of vision, which proposed that the eyes emit rays to perceive the world, a theory still debated in the early scientific revolution.</note>.

It is known that animals that go about at night have piercing sight to discern their prey in the darkness and seize it, and that the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In 17th-century physiology, "animal spirits" were thought to be extremely fine, subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note> which are in the eye, and which can spread from there, are of the nature of fire, and consequently luminous. It may happen that while the eyes are closed during sleep, these spirits, heated by the eyelids, become inflamed and set some faculty in motion, such as the imagination. For does it not happen that wood or fish bones produce some light when their heat is excited by putrefaction <note>Gassendi is referring to bioluminescence, such as "foxfire" in decaying wood or the glow of rotting sea life, which was a common scientific curiosity at the time.</note>? Why then should this heat, excited by these trapped spirits, not be able to produce some light? He then proves that the imagination alone is capable of this.

Now, we conceive even less that God would wish to concur in the frauds and illusions of the demon. There is therefore reason to believe that all these kinds of apparitions, that all these stories are false, and that they must be absolutely rejected, as being more fit to maintain the superstition and vain credulity of the people than to edify and instruct them.

These five armed horsemen, fighting for Israel, are apparently none other than Mattathias, the father of Judas Maccabeus (*a*), and four of his sons who had died. At that time, only Judas Maccabeus, Jonathan, and Simon remained of his seven <note>The author mentions seven sons, though the account in 1 Maccabees 2:1–5 specifically names five: John, Simon, Judas, Eleazar, and Jonathan.</note> sons. This could also be interpreted as five Angels sent by God to assist the Maccabees. However one interprets it, these are certain apparitions, both because of the reliability of the book in which they are recorded and because of the testimony of an entire army that saw them.

<margin>(b) Deuteronomy 18:11</margin>
From this I conclude that the Hebrews did not doubt that the spirits of the dead could return, that they did return in fact, and that they revealed to the living things that are beyond our natural knowledge. Moses expressly forbids the Israelites from consulting the dead (*b*): *There shall be no one who seeks the truth from the dead.* <note>original Latin: *Non erit qui quærat à mortuis veritatem.* This refers to the biblical prohibition against necromancy or mediumship.</note> But these apparitions did not take place in solid and material bodies; the Savior assures us of this when he said that *spirits have neither flesh nor bones.* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Luke 24:39, where Jesus distinguishes his resurrected body from that of a ghost or spirit.</note> It was often merely an ethereal <note>The author uses the term "aérienne" (aerial), implying a form made of air or spirit rather than physical matter.</note> figure that struck the senses and the imagination, like the images we see in our sleep, or which we firmly believe we see and

These spirits speak to them and warn them, or threaten them, making them see things as if they were present which, in reality, are not before their eyes but only in their imagination. This does not prevent these visions and warnings from coming from God, who—either by himself, through the ministry of his Angels, or through souls separated from the body—inspires in men whatever he judges appropriate to make known to them, or in...

If the apparitions of the souls of the dead were natural occurrences, and were a matter of their own choice, there would be few dead who would not return to visit the things or the people who were dear to them during their lives. Saint Augustine says this of his mother, Saint Monica <margin>(a)</margin>, who held for him such a tender and constant affection, and who during her life followed and sought him by sea and by land. The wicked rich man <note>A reference to the Parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16), where a rich man in hell begs to return to warn his brothers.</note> would not have failed either to come in person to find his brothers and his relatives, to inform them of the miserable state in which he found himself in hell: it is a pure grace of the mercy or the power of God, and one that he grants to very few persons—to appear after death; and it is for this reason that one must be very much on guard against everything said about them, and everything found written about them in books.

Evodius proposes various questions on this matter: If the soul, upon leaving its body, does not still preserve a certain **subtle body** <term>subtle body: a quasi-physical or "ethereal" envelope that some early Christian thinkers believed allowed the soul to be seen or moved after death</term>, with which it appears, and by means of which it is transported from one place to another? Do not the Angels themselves have a certain body? For if they are incorporeal, how can one count them? And if Samuel appeared to Saul <note>A reference to the biblical account in 1 Samuel 28, where the prophet Samuel is summoned from the dead by the medium of Endor to speak with King Saul.</note>, how could that be done if Samuel had no body? He adds: I remember very well that Profuturus, Privatus, and Servitius <note>These were former members of the monastic community at Hippo or Uzalis who had died.</note>, whom I had known in the monastery, appeared to me and spoke to me after their death; and what they told me happened. Was it their soul that appeared to me, or was it some other spirit that took their figure? He concludes from this that the soul is not absolutely without a body, since only God is truly incorporeal: *the soul, therefore, cannot be entirely without any body; this, I believe, shows that God alone is always without any body.* <note>original: "animam igitur omni corpore carere omninò non poſſe, illud, ut puto, oſtendit, quia Deus ſolus omni corpore ſemper caret."</note>

A work was recently shared with me, composed by a Premonstratensian Father <term>Premonstratensian: a Catholic religious order of canons regular founded in 1120, also known as the White Canons or Norbertines</term> from the Abbey of All Saints <note>original: "abbaye de Toussaints"</note> in the Black Forest, a very learned man. This Humbert Birck was a prominent citizen of the city of Oppenheim and the master of a country estate named Berenbach. He died in the month of November 1620, a few days before Saint Martin’s Day <note>November 11th, a traditional harvest festival and feast day</note>. On the Saturday following his funeral, people began to hear certain noises in the house where he had lived with his first wife; for at the time of his death, he had remarried and lived with another woman.

The master of this house, suspecting that it was his brother-in-law who was returning there, said to him: "If you are Humbert, my brother-in-law, strike the wall three times." At that very moment, three knocks—and only three—were heard, though usually the spirit would strike many times. He also sometimes made himself heard at the fountain, where one...

The master of the house told Humbert to strike the wall; he struck it quite gently: he said to him again: Go find a stone, and strike harder; he delayed a little, as if having gone to pick up a stone, and gave a harder blow on the wall: the master whispered to his neighbor as low as he could: Let him strike seven times; and immediately he struck seven times. I will add to this history the one told by Philip Melanchthon <note>original: "Philippe Mélancthon" — a German reformer and collaborator of Martin Luther. At first she was terrified; but her husband reassured her, and told her that he had important things to communicate to her: at the same time, he asked the Franciscan to step into the neighboring <term>heated parlor</term> <note>original: "poële" — a room kept warm by a large stove, common in Germanic and eastern French homes of the period, often serving as the primary living space.</note> while he made his wishes known to his wife. Then he begged her to have some masses said for the relief of his soul, and urged her to give him her hand without fear: as she was reluctant, he assured her she would feel no harm from it. She gave him her hand, then withdrew it without feeling any pain, but it was so marred by a burn that it remained black for the rest of her life. After this, the husband called the Franciscan back; they went out and disappeared. Melanchthon believes they were two specters: he adds that several similar examples are known, reported by very trustworthy people.

If these two men were only specters, having neither flesh nor bone, how could one of them have imprinted the black color on the hand of that widow? If they were evil spirits <note>original: "mauvais génies" — literally "evil genies," here referring to demonic entities or malevolent spirits.</note>, why did they request masses and order restitutions? Does Satan destroy his own empire, and does he inspire the living to perform good deeds and to fear the punishments with which God penalizes the sins of the wicked?

But considering the matter from another perspective, could the demon not have the intention, in these types of apparitions where he asks for masses and prayers, to foster superstition? This would be achieved by making the living believe that the masses and prayers performed after their death will protect them from the pains of hell, even if they die in the habit of crime and in impenitence. Several examples are cited of villains who appeared after their death, asking for prayers like the <term>bad rich man</term> <note>original: "mauvais riche" — a reference to the biblical parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31), in which a wealthy man is punished in the afterlife for his lack of charity and cannot be helped by the prayers of the living.</note>, and for whom prayers and masses could be of no use, given the wretched state in which they had died. Thus, in all of this, Satan seeks to establish his empire, and not to destroy or diminish it.

# CHAPTER XLII.

### *Opinions of the Jews, the Greeks, and the Latins regarding the Dead who remained without Burial.*

The ancient Hebrews, just like most other peoples, were very careful to provide burial for the dead. This is evident throughout all history. We see in the Holy Scriptures how much attention the Patriarchs <note>The biblical fathers of the Hebrew people, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> paid to this for themselves and their kin; it is well known how much praise they heaped upon the holy man Tobias <note>The central figure of the Book of Tobit, known for his acts of charity, particularly the dangerous work of burying deceased Israelites.</note>, who made it his primary act of devotion to provide burial for the dead.

<margin>(a) Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 3, chapter 25.</margin>
Josephus the historian ( *a* ) says that the Jews refuse burial only to those who have taken their own lives. Moses commanded <margin>(b) Deuteronomy 21:23.</margin> ( *b* ) that burial be given on the same day, before the setting of the sun, to one who had been executed and hung upon a cross <note>original: "attaché à la croix" — while the biblical text refers to a tree or gibbet, the author uses the term "cross" to draw a direct parallel to the crucifixion of Jesus.</note>: *Because*, he says, *he who is hung upon the wood is cursed by God; you shall take care not to defile the land that the Lord your God has given you.* This was practiced toward our Savior, who was taken down from the cross on the same day he had been placed there, only a few hours after his death.

<summary>This page introduces a discussion on the historical and religious necessity of burial, focusing on Jewish customs and the Mosaic law requiring even executed criminals to be buried before sunset.</summary>

Homer ( *a* ), speaking of the inhumanity of Achilles, who dragged Hector’s body behind his chariot, says that he dishonored and outraged the earth by this barbaric conduct. They further believe that after death, the souls of the wicked are clothed in a kind of casing or overcoat <note>original: "surtout" — a term for an outer garment, here implying a spiritual covering that allows the soul to feel physical torment.</note>, with which they grow accustomed to suffering the punishments due to them; and that the souls of the righteous are clothed in a resplendent body and a luminous garment, with which they grow accustomed to the brilliance of the glory that awaits them.

Origen <note>An early Christian theologian and scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for his complex views on the soul and its pre-existence.</note> ( *b* ) acknowledges that Plato, in his dialogue on the soul <note>Referring to the *Phaedo*, where Plato discusses the immortality of the soul and why some spirits might remain near their graves.</note>, puts forward that the images and shadows of the dead sometimes appear near their tombs. Origen concludes from this that these shadows and images must have a cause that produces them; and this cause, according to him, can only be the soul of the dead, which is clothed in a subtle body—similar to that of light—upon which they are carried as if in a chariot where they appear to the living. Celsus <note>A 2nd-century Greek philosopher and early critic of Christianity.</note> argued that the apparitions of Jesus Christ after his resurrection were nothing but the effects of a struck and biased imagination, which formed for itself the objects of its illusions based on its own desires.
