Here is a singular example of a deceased man who refused burial, recognizing himself as unworthy of it. Agathias <note>Agathias Scholasticus (c. 530–582 AD), a Byzantine historian and poet.</note> relates (a) that several pagan philosophers, unable to accept the doctrine of the unity of a single God <note>A reference to the Christian monotheism promoted by the Byzantine state, which conflicted with their Neoplatonist views.</note>, resolved to travel from Constantinople to the court of Khosrow <note>Khosrow I, the Sassanid King of Persia, known for his interest in philosophy.</note>, King of Persia, who was spoken of as a humane Prince and a lover of literature. Simplicius of Cilicia, Eulamius the Phrygian, Priscian the Lydian <note>OCR: Protan</note>, Hermias <note>OCR: Hermene</note> and Philogenes of Phoenicia, and Isidore of Gaza thus traveled to the court of Khosrow and were well received there; but they soon perceived that this country was far more corrupt than Greece, and they resolved to return to Constantinople, where Justinian then reigned.

As they were on their way, they found a corpse without burial, felt pity for it, and had their servants place it in the earth. The following night, this man appeared to one of them and told him not to bury one who was not worthy of receiving burial; that the earth abhorred one who had defiled <note>The original French 'fouillé' is likely a transcription error for 'souillé,' meaning defiled or polluted.</note> his own mother. The next day, they found the same corpse cast out of the earth, and understood that he had defiled himself with an incest that rendered him unworthy of the honor of burial—even though such crimes were common in Persia and were not regarded with the same horror as in other countries.

# ->ON SPIRITS<-

<margin>Y ij</margin>

The Greeks and the Romans believed that the souls of the dead came to taste the offerings left on their tombs, especially honey and wine. They believed that spirits <note>The original French uses "démons," referring to the Greek "daimon"—intermediate beings between gods and mortals, not necessarily evil spirits.</note> delighted in the smoke and scent of sacrifices, in music, in the blood of victims, and in intimacy with women. These spirits were thought to be tied for a time to certain places or buildings which they haunted and where they appeared. It was believed that souls, once separated from their earthly bodies, retained a "subtle body" <term>subtle body: a refined, airy, or luminous substance that allowed the soul to maintain its shape and visibility after death</term>—a slender, ethereal form that preserved the likeness of the person they had once animated. These forms were said to be luminous, resembling the stars. Furthermore, souls were thought to retain the inclinations and feelings they had held during life, continuing to care for those they loved and pursuing those who had wronged or hated them. Thus, Virgil describes a furious Dido threatening to haunt the treacherous Aeneas (*a*):

> *I shall follow you with black fires, though I am absent;*
> *And when cold death has drawn my limbs away from my soul,*
> *I shall be present as a ghost in every place: you will pay the penalty, wicked man.*
<note>original: "Sequar atris ignibus absens; / Et cùm frigida mors animâ subduxerit artus, / Omnibus umbra locis adero: dabis, improbe, pœnas." — Virgil, Aeneid, Book IV, lines 384-386.</note>

When the soul of Patroclus appeared to Achilles (*b*), it possessed his voice, his stature, his eyes, and his clothing, but it lacked a palpable body. Similarly, when Odysseus descended into the underworld, he saw there the divine Her— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the author is likely referring to Hercules (Hercule).</note>

Saint Irenaeus (a) teaches, as a doctrine received from the Lord, that souls not only exist after the death of the body—without, however, passing from one body to another, as those who accept <term>metempsychosis: the movement of a soul into a new body after death, often called reincarnation</term> believe—but that they retain the shape of the body. He suggests they remain near that body, like faithful guardians, and remember what they did and did not do in this life. These Fathers <note>A term for the influential early Christian theologians whose writings established the intellectual foundations of the Church.</note> thus believed in the return of souls, their appearances, and their attachment to their bodies. However, we do not adopt their opinion regarding the <term>corporeality: the state of having a physical body or material substance</term> of souls; we are persuaded that they can appear by the permission of God, independently of any matter or physical substance of their own.

# CHAPTER XLIII.

## *Examination of what the returning dead request from or reveal to the living.*

Apparitions occur either through good angels, or through demons, or through the souls of the deceased, or through the living appearing to other people who are still alive.
Good angels usually bring only good news and announce nothing but happiness; or if they announce future misfortunes, it is in order to engage men to prevent them, or to turn them away through <term>penance: an act of devotion or self-denial performed to show sorrow for sins</term>, or to profit from the evils that God sends them through the exercise of patience and <term>resignation: the humble acceptance of God's will</term> to His orders.

Philip, Chancellor of the Church of Paris, maintained that the <term>plurality of benefices: the practice of one person holding multiple church offices and collecting the income from all of them</term> was permitted. A few days after his death, Bishop William, while praying at night after <term>Matins: the first of the daily prayer services, usually held in the early hours before dawn</term> in his Cathedral, saw appearing before him the figure of a hideous and frightening man; he made the sign of the cross and said to him: "If you are sent by God, speak." He spoke and said: "I am that wretched chancellor, who has been condemned to eternal torment." The Bishop having asked him the cause, he replied: "I am condemned: 1st, for not having distributed to the poor the surplus of my benefices; 2nd, for having maintained that it was permitted to possess several of them; 3rd, for having wallowed for some days in the crime of <term>incontinence: in this historical context, a lack of self-restraint, specifically regarding sexual purity or lust</term>."

Afterwards, they asked for the name of the person who was to succeed the Emperor Valens. The ring touched the four letters, **T E O D**, which they interpreted as referring to Theodosius, the second secretary to the Emperor Valens. ...a living person, without either one knowing how, when, or where these images are formed in our mind. It may also happen that a dead person appears to the living without being aware of it, and reveals hidden and future things, the truth and reality of which are revealed by the event itself. When a living man appears in a dream to another man, we do not say that his body or his soul appeared to him, but simply that such a person appeared to him. Why then can we not say that the dead appear without bodies and without souls, but simply that their figure presents itself to the mind and imagination of the living person?

<margin>(a) <note>original: "Aug. de cura gerend. pro mort. cap. 17. pag 529."</note> Augustine, *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 17, page 529.</margin>
Saint Augustine, in the book he composed on the care that must be taken for the dead (a), says that a holy monk named John appeared to a pious woman who ardently desired to see him. The fact is taken from the *Treatise on Superstitions* by the <term>Reverend Father Le Brun<note>original: "R. P. le Brun"; Pierre Le Brun (1661–1729) was a French priest and historian who wrote extensively on the history of religious practices and superstitions.</note></term> (a), and is endowed with everything that can make it incontestable; I will report it only in summary. On Friday, the first day of May 1705, around five o'clock in the evening, Denis Misanger de la Richardiere, eighteen years old, was attacked by an extraordinary illness, which began with a kind of lethargy: he was given all the aid that medicine and surgery could provide; he then fell into a kind of fury or <term>convulsion<note>original: "convulsion"; a medical term for involuntary muscle contractions, often interpreted in the 18th century as a sign of spiritual or physical crisis.</note></term>, and they were forced to hold him and have him guarded by five or six people, for fear that he would throw himself out the windows, or break his head against the wall: the <term>emetic<note>original: "émétique"; a medicine used to induce vomiting, a common treatment in this period to purge "excess bile."</note></term> given to him caused him to throw up a large amount of bile, and he remained fairly calm for four or five days.

At the end of the month of May, he was sent to the countryside to take the air: new accidents occurred to him, so unusual that it was judged that he was <term>bewitched<note>original: "ensorcellé"; under the influence of a magical spell.</note></term>; and what confirmed this conjecture is that he never had a fever, and that he preserved all his strength, notwithstanding all his ills and the violent remedies that had been given to him.

How was the shepherd able to cast a <term>spell<note>original: "sort"; a magical curse. # CHAPTER XLV.
## *Reasonings on Apparitions.*

After having spoken for quite some time about apparitions, and after having established their truth as much as possible by the authority of the <term>Scriptures<note>Referring to the Bible as the primary evidence for supernatural phenomena.</note></term>, by examples, and by reasoning, we must now pass judgment on the causes, the means, and the reasons for these apparitions, and respond to the objections that may be raised to destroy their reality, or at least to cast doubt upon them.

<meta>This page continues the theoretical discussion introduced at the end of Chapter XLV, moving from the specific case of M. de la Richardière to a broader theological examination of how spirits manifest to the living.</meta>

->APPARITIONS<-

We have assumed that apparitions were the work of Angels, demons, or the souls of the deceased; we are not speaking of the apparitions of God himself; his will, his operations, and his power are beyond our reach. We recognize that He can do all that He wills, that His will is almighty, and that He places Himself, when He wishes, above the laws He has made. As for the apparitions of living men to other living men, they are of a different nature from those we propose to examine here; we shall nonetheless speak of them hereafter.

Whichever system one follows regarding the nature of Angels, demons, or souls separated from the body—whether one holds them to be purely <term>spiritual substances<note>In scholastic philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself. A "purely spiritual" substance has no physical matter or extension in space.</note></term>, as the Christian Church holds today, or whether one gives them an <term>aerial body<note>original: "corps aérien." Many early theologians and philosophers believed that spirits were not "nothing," but were composed of a very fine, thin matter like air or light.</note></term>—subtle and invisible, as several have taught—it appears almost as difficult to make a subtle and aerial body palpable, perceptible, and thick, as it is to condense the air and make it appear as a solid and sensible body. This occurs, for instance, when the Angels appeared to <term>Abraham and Lot<note>Refers to Genesis 18 and 19, where angels appeared as men to announce the birth of Isaac and the destruction of Sodom.</note></term>, the Angel Raphael to <term>Tobias<note>From the Book of Tobit; Raphael disguised himself as a human travel companion to guide Tobias.</note></term>, whom he led into <term>Media<note>An ancient region in present-day Iran.</note></term>, or when the demon appeared to Jesus Christ and led him onto a high mountain and upon the pinnacle of the temple of Jerusalem, or when Moses appeared with Elijah on <term>Mount Tabor<note>The traditional site of the Transfiguration of Jesus.</note></term>; for these...

apparitions are certain according to the <term>Scriptures<note>The author uses the Bible as his primary historical evidence to argue that spirits can truly manifest in the physical world.</note></term>.

If one wishes to claim that these apparitions were only in the imagination and the minds of those who saw, or believed they saw, Angels, demons, or souls separated from the body—much as happens every day during sleep, and sometimes while awake, when one is deeply preoccupied with certain objects, or struck by things that one ardently desires or extraordinarily fears; as when <term>Ajax<note>A reference to the tragedy by Sophocles. Driven mad by Athena, the Greek hero Ajax slaughters a flock of livestock, hallucinating that they are his rivals Ulysses and Agamemnon.</note></term>, believing he saw Ulysses and Agamemnon, or Menelaus, fell upon animals and slaughtered them, believing he was killing these two men—his enemies—upon whom he was dying to take his revenge.

In this supposition, the apparition will be no less difficult to explain. There was neither prejudice, nor a troubled imagination, nor any prior passion that would have led Abraham to imagine he saw three persons, to whom he gave food, to whom he spoke, and who promised him the birth of a son—something he was hardly thinking of at the time. The three Apostles who saw Moses conversing with Jesus Christ on <term>Mount Tabor<note>The site of the Transfiguration, where Peter, James, and John witnessed Jesus speaking with the long-deceased prophets Moses and Elijah.</note></term> were not at all prepared for this apparition; there was no passion of fear, love, vengeance, ambition, or any other that struck their imagination to dispose them to see Moses, just as there was none in Abraham when he perceived the three Angels who appeared to him.

Often in sleep we see, or we believe we see, what has struck us greatly while awake, or what we strongly desire; sometimes we represent to ourselves things we have never thought of, and even things that are repugnant to us, which present themselves to our minds despite ourselves. No one thinks to seek the causes of these sorts of representations: they are attributed to chance, or to some disposition of the <term>humors<note>In older medical theory, the "humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were bodily fluids believed to influence health and temperament. An imbalance was often thought to cause vivid dreams or hallucinations.</note></term>, or of the blood, or of the brain, or even of the place where one is lying, or the way in which the body is positioned in bed. But none of this is applicable to the apparitions of Angels, demons, or spirits, when these apparitions are accompanied and followed by actions, speeches, predictions, and real effects, preceded and foretold by those who appear.

If one has recourse to a so-called <term>fascination<note>In the 18th century, "fascination" often referred to a kind of sensory deception or "glamour" where the eyes are tricked into seeing something that isn't there, or failing to see something that is.</note></term> of the eyes or other senses, which sometimes make us believe that we see and hear what we do not see and hear, or that we do not see or hear what passes before our eyes or what strikes our ears; as when the soldiers sent to arrest <term>Elisha<note>A reference to 2 Kings 6:18-20, where the prophet Elisha prays for his enemies to be struck with "blindness"—likely a confusion of the mind—so they do not recognize him as they speak to him.</note></term> spoke to him and saw him before knowing who he was, or when the inhabitants of <term>Sodom<note>In Genesis 19:11, the men of the city were struck with blindness by angels, preventing them from finding the door to Lot's house.</note></term> could not recognize the door of Lot, even though it was right before their eyes, or when the disciples at <term>Emmaus<note>Referring to Luke 24:13-35, where two disciples walk and dine with the resurrected Jesus but are supernaturally prevented from recognizing him until the end of the encounter.</note></term> did not recognize Jesus Christ...

One might tell me that it is useless to have recourse to the miraculous and the supernatural, if one recognizes in spiritual substances a natural power to make themselves visible, whether by condensing the air, or by producing a massive and palpable body, or by reviving some dead body to which these spirits restore life and movement for a certain time.

I grant all this; but I dare to maintain that this is possible neither for an Angel, nor for a demon, nor for any spiritual substance, whatever it may be. The soul can certainly produce thoughts, volitions, and desires within itself; it can certainly impress movements upon its body and restrain its impulses and agitations; but how does it do so? Philosophy can hardly explain it, except by saying that by virtue of the union it has with its body, God, through an effect of His wisdom, has given it the power to act upon its <term>humors<note>In early modern medicine and philosophy, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament. The author is suggesting the soul influences the physical state of the body through these fluids.</note></term>, upon its organs, and to impress certain movements upon them; but there is reason to believe that it only operates all this as an <term>occasional cause<note>This refers to a philosophical theory called Occasionalism, popularized by Nicolas Malebranche. It argues that created things (like souls) do not truly cause effects; rather, God brings about the effect on the "occasion" of the soul's will.</note></term>, and that it is God, as the **primary**, necessary, immediate, and essential **cause**, who produces all the movements of the body that occur in nature.

Neither the Angel nor the demon has any more privilege in this regard over matter than the human soul has over its own body. They can neither modify matter, nor change it, nor impress actions and movements upon it except by the power of God, and with His necessary and immediate cooperation: our reasoning does not permit us to judge otherwise: there is no physical proportion between spirit and body: these two substances cannot act mutually and immediately upon one another; they can only act occasionally, in de-

And if we once open the door to this <term>fascination<note>In this historical context, "fascination" refers to a supernatural delusion or a demonic "glamour" that tricks the senses into seeing something that isn't there.</note></term>, everything that appears supernatural and miraculous will become uncertain and doubtful. People will say that the wonders recounted in the Old and New Testaments are, for those who witnessed them or to whom they occurred, nothing but illusions and fascinations; and where do such principles not lead? This leads to doubting everything, to denying everything, and to believing that God, in concert with the devil, leads us into error and fascinates our eyes and our other senses, making us believe that we see, hear, and know things that are neither present to our eyes, nor known to our mind, nor supported by our reasoning, since the very principles of reasoning are thereby overturned.

We must therefore resort to the solid and unshakable principles of religion, which teach us:

1st. That Angels, demons, and souls separated from the body are pure spirits, detached from all matter.

2nd. functions, which belong only to matter and to living and animated bodies.

For either spiritual substances are united to the bodies that appear, or they are not. If they are not united to them, how can they move them and make them act, walk, speak, reason, and eat? If they are united to them, they are then but a whole, a single individual with them; and how can they separate from them after having been united? Do they take them up and cast them off at will, as one takes off a garment or a mask? This would suppose that they are masters of appearing or disappearing; which is not the case, since every apparition occurs solely by the order or by the permission of God. Are these bodies that appear only the instruments that Angels, demons, or souls use to frighten, to warn, to punish, or to instruct the person or persons to whom they appear? This is indeed the most reasonable thing that can be said regarding these apparitions: the <term>exorcisms<note>In this context, the author refers to formal liturgical rites used by the Church to address or dispel supernatural disturbances.</note></term> of the Church fall directly only upon the agent and the mover of these apparitions, and not upon the phantom that appears, nor upon the primary author, who is God, who orders or permits it.

souls, of demons, of goblins <note>original: "folets"; these are mischievous spirits or sprites often found in folklore.</note>, of possessions, and obsessions <note>In historical theology, "obsession" refers to a demon harassing a person from the outside, whereas "possession" refers to the demon controlling them from within.</note>.

One must admit that out of a hundred of these alleged apparitions, barely two will be true: the ancients are no more believable in this regard than the moderns, since they were at least as credulous as people are in our century, or rather, they were more credulous than we are today.

I agree that the vain credulity of the common people and the love for what seems marvelous and extraordinary have produced an infinite number of false stories on the subject we are treating. There are two pitfalls to avoid here: too much credulity, and an excessive difficulty in believing what is above the ordinary course of nature. Just as one should not draw a general conclusion from a particular case, nor say that everything is false because there are some false stories, so one should not always assert that a specific story in particular is invented for pleasure simply because there are a great many of the latter kind. It is permissible to examine, to test, and to choose; one should only render judgment with full knowledge of the case. A story may be false in several of its circumstances and yet be true in its essence.

The history of the Great Flood and that of the crossing of the Red Sea are certain in themselves, and in the simple and straightforward <note>The original "naïf" here implies a natural, unadorned, or sincere quality rather than "naive" in the modern sense.</note> account given by Moses.

Josephus the historian <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide essential context for the biblical era.</note> greatly embellished the history of Moses; Christian authors have added much to that of Josephus; the Mohammedans <note>An archaic term used by the author to refer to Muslims.</note> have altered several points of the sacred history of the Old and New Testaments: must we, for that reason, call these histories into question? It is not permitted to dispute the truth of the apparitions recorded in the Old and New Testaments, but it is permitted to explain them: for example, it is said that the Lord appeared to Abraham in the valley of Mamre (a), that he entered the tent of Abraham, and that he promised him the birth of a son: however, it is agreed that he received three Angels, who went from there to Sodom. In 1628, Desbordes, a valet to the Duke of Lorraine, Charles IV <note>Charles IV (1604–1675) was a Duke of Lorraine known for his long and tumultuous reign during the Thirty Years' War.</note>, was accused of having hastened the death of Princess Christine de Salm <note>Duchess of Lorraine and mother of Charles IV; her death was a significant event in the ducal court.</note>, the wife of Duke François II and mother of Duke Charles IV, and of having caused various people to suffer illnesses that physicians attributed to <term>sorcery</term> <note>The original term "maléfices" refers to harmful magic or hexes intended to cause physical injury or death.</note>. It was further said that on another occasion he had ordered the figures on a tapestry to detach themselves and present themselves in the middle of the room.

# CHAPTER XLIX.

->*Conclusion of the Treatise on Apparitions.*<-

After having set forth my opinion on the apparitions of Angels, of demons, of the souls of the departed, and even of living men to other living men; and having spoken of magic, oracles, <term>obsessions</term> <note>In traditional demonology, "obsession" refers to a demon attacking a person from the outside, whereas "possession" involves the demon inhabiting the body.</note> and possessions of the demon, of <term>playful spirits</term> <note>original: "esprits folets." These are domestic spirits or hobgoblins, similar to the English Robin Goodfellow or Puck, often thought to be more mischievous than truly evil.</note> and familiars, of male and female sorcerers, of spectres that predict the future, and of those that infest houses; after having proposed the objections raised against apparitions and having responded to them as solidly as I could, I believe I can conclude that—although this matter suffers from very great difficulties, both regarding the heart of the matter (I mean the truth and reality of apparitions in general) and the manner in which they occur—nonetheless, one cannot reasonably disagree that there are true apparitions of all the kinds we have just discussed. However, one must also admit that there are a very great number of others that are highly contestable, and still others that are clearly the work of trickery, the malice of men, the cleverness of <term>charlatans</term> <note>At this time, "charlatan" referred not just to medical frauds, but to street performers and traveling tricksters who used stage magic to deceive the public.</note>, and the dexterity of <term>sleight-of-hand performers</term>.

...converse, drink, and eat, as did the Angels who appeared to Abraham (a), and the one who appeared (b) to young Tobiah and led him to Rages? <note>In the Book of Tobit, the Archangel Raphael disguises himself as a man to guide Tobit's son, Tobiah, to the city of Rages in Media.</note> Is all this done through the natural power of these spirits? Did God grant them this power at their creation, and has He committed Himself—by virtue of His natural laws and as a result of His intimate and essential action upon the creature in His capacity as Creator—to imprint, upon the occasion of the will of these spirits, certain movements in the air and in the bodies they wish to move, condense, and cause to act? This would be in the same proportion as He willed that, by virtue of the union of the soul to a living body, this soul should imprint upon that body movements proportioned to its own will. This is despite the fact that, naturally, there is no natural proportion between matter and spirit, and that according to the laws of physics, one cannot act upon the other—except insofar as the <term>First Cause</term> <note>The "First Cause" is a philosophical concept referring to the initial cause of all things, traditionally identified as God.</note>, the Creator Being, has willed to subject Himself to creating this movement and producing these effects at the instance of man’s will; movements which, without this, would be considered supernatural.

<page-num>421</page-num>
<header># OF SPIRITS.</header>

can one understand that the soul itself might be material & extended? <note>Original: *étendue*. In the philosophy of this era, "extension" was the primary quality of matter—the fact that it occupies physical space. By contrast, the soul was traditionally defined as having no extension.</note> In this latter case, would it act upon itself, & give itself the motion to think, or will this motion be the thought, or will it produce the thought? will this thinking matter <note>Original: *matiere pensante*. This refers to a controversial 18th-century debate over whether thought is a spiritual substance or merely a complex arrangement of physical matter.</note> think always, or only sometimes? & when it has ceased to think, who is it that will make it think again? will it be God? will it be itself? can an agent as simple as the soul act upon itself, & reproduce itself in some way by thinking, after having ceased to think?

My Reader will say that I leave him here in a state of confusion, & that instead of giving him enlightenment on the appearances of spirits, I spread doubts & uncertainty on this subject: I agree; but I prefer to doubt prudently, rather than to assert what I do not know. And if I hold to what my religion teaches me about the nature of souls, of Angels & of demons, I will say that being purely spiritual, it is impossible for them to appear clothed in a body, of whatever kind it may be, without a miracle; assuming, however, that God did not create them naturally capable of these operations, in subordination to his sovereignly powerful will, which only rarely allows them to put into execution this faculty of making themselves seen bodily to mortals.

> *When I was with you, I was there by the will of God: it seemed to you that I drank and ate; but as for me, I use an invisible food, which is unknown to men.* <note>This quote is from the Book of Tobit (12:18-19). ...acted and walked like men, it was not out of any need they had to drink or to eat to sustain themselves and to live, but for the fulfillment of the designs of God, who willed that they should appear to men, acting, drinking, and eating, as the Angel Raphael notes (a): *When I was with you, I was there by the will of God: it seemed to you that I drank and ate; but for my part, I make use of an invisible food, which is unknown to men.* <note>This passage from the Book of Tobit explains that the angel's physical actions were an appearance or "vision" intended for human benefit, rather than a biological necessity.</note>

It is true that we do not know what the food of Angels—who are purely spiritual substances—might be, nor what became of this food that Raphael and the three Angels whom Abraham entertained in his tent <note>A reference to Genesis 18, where Abraham receives three visitors; in Christian theology, these are often interpreted as angels or a manifestation of God.</note> took, or seemed to take, in the company of men. But there are so many other things in nature that are unknown and incomprehensible to us, that we must certainly take comfort in not knowing how the apparitions of Angels, demons, and souls separated from the body <note>Original: *ames séparées*. This is a technical theological term for the human soul after death when it is no longer joined to the physical body.</note> occur.
